Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of the soundness test of cement?

options.html: To measure the early hardening ability of cement paste.
To evaluate the fineness and particle size distribution of cement.
To check for volume stability by detecting expansion due to free lime.
To check for clear ringing sound when two hardened samples are struck together.

questions.solution:
(c)
Soundness test is essential to check that the concrete does not undergo large change in volume
after setting.
The main cause for unsoundness in Portland cement is the hydration of the uncombined lime
encased within the cement particles. Exposed, finely ground, free lime in small percentages,
hydrates before the cement sets and produces no injurious effect. The uncombined lime in cement
is a result of either under burning the clinker or of excess lime in the raw materials. Freshly
ground cement is often unsound due to the presence of uncombined lime. Cement is thus allowed
to aerate for two to three weeks, allowing the lime to hydrate, to overcome unsoundness.

Which of the following processes are involved in chemical weathering?
questions.solution:
(a, c, d)
• Mechanical weathering or physical disintegration processes are as follows:
1. Plant roots 2. Frost 3. Thermal expansion 4. Abrasion
• Chemical weathering processes are as follows:
1. Oxidation 2. Hydration 3. Carbonation 4. Hydrolysis 5. Leaching
• Leaching: In this process, some minerals are dissolved out of the rocks and deposited separately causing decomposition
• Hydration: In this process, water combines with rich minerals and forms new compounds.
• Hydrolysis: It is a chemical weathering and affects silicates minerals.

For a non-uniform velocity distribution in an open-channel cross-section, which of the following relations between the kinetic-energy correction factor α and the momentum-correction factor β is correct?
questions.solution:
(c)
The coefficients α and β account for non-uniformity in velocity distribution across an open-channel
section. As the velocity distribution becomes more uneven, the values of α and β increase and
generally satisfy α > β > 1. Larger and deeper channels with more regular sections tend to show
lower values of these coefficients, whereas small or irregular channels may exhibit comparatively
higher values. In natural and compound channels, α and β can reach significantly large values depending on flow irregularities.
Under ideal conditions of uniform velocity distribution, both coefficients become unity, i.e., α = β
= 1. For engineering analysis, this unity assumption is often acceptable in straight prismatic channels
or when the flow is nearly uniform. However, in practical natural channels, approximate ranges
of α and β are recommended to account for non-uniform flow behaviour.
